card.hook: Two stone pagodas stand in one courtyard, and they couldn't look more different: one richly carved, one plain as toast. That contrast is the whole fun of Bulguksa.
card.stand_here: Stand about 20 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. That puts the temple's stonework and buildings right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the stairway, gate and courtyard, where everything is close and fills the frame. Use 1x for general shots, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out carvings and rooflines.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stone, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and stone both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or later in the afternoon. There are usually fewer people in your shots and the light is softer.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the water's edge of the lily pond facing the Beomyeongru pavilion, then turn your back to it so the pavilion and its reflection sit behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it. The first flight of stone stairs up to the main gate (Jahamun) also works, with the gate framed over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand in the middle of the main courtyard between Dabotap and Seokgatap, with the main hall (Daeungjeon) behind you, and suggest 0.5x so both pagodas and the hall fit.
card.rules_and_safety: The Lotus Flower Bridge and Seven Treasures Bridge are closed to walkers, so shoot them from where you can see them. Photos are generally fine outdoors but not inside the halls with the Buddha statues, and this is a working temple, so dress and behave respectfully.
card.challenge: Take one portrait of each pagoda on its own, then hunt for the angle that squeezes both into a single shot.
card.good_to_know: Dabotap is 10.4 metres tall and Seokgatap is 8.2 metres tall. The present temple was begun in 751 and finished in 774, and the famous stonework is preserved from the original Silla construction. The wooden buildings burned during the Imjin wars and were rebuilt later. Bulguksa joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 20 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. That puts the temple's stonework and buildings right in front of you.

card.hook: You've climbed up to about 750 metres on Tohamsan, and the ridges roll away toward the East Sea like folded green blankets. Here's the twist: the grotto itself is a no-photos zone inside, so this view is your picture.
card.stand_here: Stand on the 석굴암전망대 lookout terrace on the Seokguram approach, near the grotto area. Face out over Tohamsan's ridges toward the East Sea. The grotto area is a short way to the west, so turn that way for context.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the ridges and the lookout. Go 0.5x to squeeze in more mountains, or 2x to 5x (if your phone has them) to pick out the ridge lines and the faraway sea.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then tap the ridges and slide darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Late morning, when one guide says the sun lights the grotto entrance directly. Sunrise over the sea is popular too, but check the official site for current visiting times first.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stone stairs in front of the wooden grotto building, which a Gyeongju guide names as the commemorative photo spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the building behind you. The guide doesn't say which way to face, so check the framing when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Wave over a friendly passer-by and show them the stairs and the wooden building beyond; the exact spot for them to stand isn't confirmed, so test a frame or two.
card.rules_and_safety: No photography inside the grotto, so no selfies with the Buddha. The bus road up is winding (one reviewer found it a bit scary in rain), and trail work has been reported, so check conditions and take your time.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the layered ridges where you can count at least three ridge lines before the sea.
card.good_to_know: Seokguram is a small hermitage and granite grotto, about 3 kilometres from Bulguksa. Both share a World Heritage listing from 1995. Work began in 751 and finished in 774, in the Unified Silla period.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the 석굴암전망대 lookout terrace on the Seokguram approach, near the grotto area. Face out over Tohamsan's ridges toward the East Sea. The grotto area is a short way to the west, so turn that way for context.

card.hook: Picture a pale stone bottle, only 9.17 metres tall, peeking out between tree trunks while everyone else queues on the lawn. That's Cheomseongdae from the quiet side.
card.stand_here: Stand in 계림, the wooded path a few minutes' walk from the observatory, and look back toward the tower, which lies to the north-east. Use the trunks and branches as a frame around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the trees and the tower together. Then try 2x to pull the tower in closer between the trunks.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tower, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the pale stone keeps its detail against the sky (if it looks gloomy among the trees, tap again and go brighter).
card.best_time: Sunny afternoons in autumn are lovely here, when the cosmos and the forest work together. Peak season brings crowds to the front of the tower, so this shady side is the calmer choice.
card.selfie_here: In summer, stand among the tall sunflowers in the field in front of the tower in the late afternoon. Use the front camera, keep the flowers close to you, and frame the tower so it peeks through the stalks.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand off to one side of the tower on the lawn, not straight in front, so the whole tower and the flower field fit in the frame (the tower is fenced off, so they can't go right up to it).
card.rules_and_safety: Climbing the tower isn't allowed, and staff ask people to keep off the grass, especially the pink muhly, so stay on the paths. Drone flying typically needs prior approval, so check the official site for current rules.
card.challenge: Find the square window on the south side of the tower and get it into your shot without cutting off the top.
card.good_to_know: Cheomseongdae was built as an observatory in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632–647) and is thought to be the oldest surviving one in Asia. Its body is made of 365 cut stones, usually taken to stand for the days of the year. It became a national treasure in 1962.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in 계림, the wooded path a few minutes' walk from the observatory, and look back toward the tower, which lies to the north-east. Use the trunks and branches as a frame around it.

card.hook: Picture a long wooden bridge with a tiled roof and a gatehouse at each end, then picture it doubled in the water below. That's the shot you're after, and it's all there from the stream bank.
card.stand_here: Walk down to the stream bank and find the stepping stones right in front of Woljeonggyo. The phone icon on the map sits there, at the middle of the bridge's length. Face the bridge so both gate pavilions are in the frame, and use the nearest stones as your foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x, which fits the whole bridge and its reflection. If you're too close for both gate pavilions, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for roof tiles and painted details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the bridge along the upper third, so the lower part is left for the water and its reflection.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, when the sky still has some colour and the bridge lights are on. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady so the shot doesn't blur.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone crossing in front of the bridge entrance with Woljeonggyo behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone a bit low so the roofline fits over your shoulder. The crossing is narrow with water alongside, so keep out of other people's way.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the public bank across the stream, where the whole bridge fits in one frame, while you pose in front of the bridge on dry ground rather than on the wet stones.
card.rules_and_safety: Wet stepping stones can be very slippery, so skip them when the water is high or fast and shoot from the bank instead. Don't enter the river areas if access is blocked, the current is strong, or there's ice.
card.challenge: Get the bridge, its reflection and one stepping stone all in a single frame, with the roofline dead level.
card.good_to_know: Woljeonggyo was first built in 760 A.D., in the Unified Silla period, and was later lost. The bridge you see now was rebuilt and opened in April 2018, and it's a little over 66 metres long. The upper floors of the gatehouses hold exhibits on how it was rebuilt, but opening times vary and the interiors may close earlier, so check locally.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk down to the stream bank and find the stepping stones right in front of Woljeonggyo. The phone icon on the map sits there, at the middle of the bridge's length. Face the bridge so both gate pavilions are in the frame, and use the nearest stones as your foreground.

card.hook: Walk the edge of Anapji and the picture keeps changing: open water, then trees, then one of three little islands, then a timber pavilion sliding into view. Don't stop at the first nice angle.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, facing the third restored pavilion. You get there by walking clockwise from the entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole pond and its islands in. Switch to 1x for a natural view. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out a single roof against the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the screen, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky and any lights don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning or around dusk gives softer light and calmer water, which is great for reflections. The pavilions mirrored in the pond look most striking after dark. Check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements.
card.selfie_here: Try the Imhaejeon site inside the Donggung Palace grounds, near the pond. Use the front camera at 0.5x and see if you can fit the pavilion over your shoulder. Have a quick look on site to find the best angle.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a managed heritage site within Gyeongju National Park, so access arrangements may apply. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo of each of the three islands as you walk round, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: King Munmu had this pond built in 674 CE, and it was part of the Silla palace complex. Digs between 1975 and 1986 turned up almost 33,000 relics, from roof tiles to gilt bronze Buddha figures. About 730 of them are on show in the Anapji Exhibition Hall at the Gyeongju National Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, facing the third restored pavilion. You get there by walking clockwise from the entrance.

card.hook: Here's a museum where you can take photos without a glass case bouncing your own face back at you. Lots of the pieces sit outdoors in the open air, so the grounds are the real show.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Gyeongju National Museum grounds, so the museum is all around you. Walk a little way until the building or display piece fits your screen, then turn back and take the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for most views. Go to 0.5x for the long building fronts and wide open grounds, and 2x for details on the outdoor display pieces.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building edges with them so the walls look nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the sun is lower and the light on the outdoor pieces is softer. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the Dongbu sunflower fields, between the museum and Donggung Palace & Wolji Pond. A visitor called them a very popular selfie spot when in bloom in October. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the flowers over your shoulder. The museum probably won't be in this one.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash and selfie sticks are not allowed in the galleries, so keep the selfie stick in your bag indoors. Photo rules can differ from room to room, so look for signs and ask staff if you're unsure.
card.challenge: Find an outdoor piece, put it in the front of your photo with the museum behind it, and leave a strip of sky on top. Bonus points if nobody walks through.
card.good_to_know: Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom, and this museum is the place to see what Silla left behind, including several crowns. It also holds the Emille Bell, which legend says rings with the voice of a child sacrificed in its casting. The museum began in 1945, the main building went up in 1968, and it took its present name in 1975.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Gyeongju National Museum grounds, so the museum is all around you. Walk a little way until the building or display piece fits your screen, then turn back and take the shot.

card.hook: Stand at the foot of Gyeongju Tower and you'll be craning your neck like you're counting floors on a 30-storey block. It's 82 metres of slim tower, and the trick is getting all of it into your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Gyeongju Tower in Gyeongju Expo Park. The phone icon on the map sits right at your position, so you'll be looking up at it from close range. Face the tower, then step back as far as the surroundings allow for a calmer, straighter view.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x when you're close to the base and want the whole height in one frame. Switch to 1x from further back for a more natural look, and try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details near the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn your phone upright, switch on the gridlines, and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands up straight, with some sky left above the top.
card.best_time: Try soft morning or late-afternoon light, and a clear sky if you can get one, since it makes the cleanest background. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Try the circular square beside the tower, standing on the centre of its paving, which repeats the Silla mask-tile pattern. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the tower over your shoulder. Nobody confirms the tower lines up behind you from there, so check the framing on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: If you want to go up the tower, check the official site before you go, as access and opening arrangements can change.
card.challenge: Take three shots: one wide with the surroundings, one upright of the full height, and one close-up of the structure against the sky. Then pick a winner.
card.good_to_know: Gyeongju Tower is an observation tower in Gyeongju Expo Park, and it's 82 metres tall. It was completed on 14 August 2007, together with the Gyeongju Expo Culture Center.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Gyeongju Tower in Gyeongju Expo Park. The phone icon on the map sits right at your position, so you'll be looking up at it from close range. Face the tower, then step back as far as the surroundings allow for a calmer, straighter view.

card.hook: Picture a wooden pagoda about 80 m tall, one of the tallest things in East Asia, and then picture a big open field with just its footprint left. That's Hwangnyongsa, and the emptiness is the whole charm.
card.stand_here: Walk in among the pagoda foundations at Hwangnyongsa and stand right at the subject. Face along the central axis of the temple layout, with the stone bases in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole field of foundation stones in. Then go to 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pagoda model or the History and Culture Center in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line and a big stone base in the lower third, then tap the stones and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go early morning for fewer people and softer light. Late afternoon is lovely too, with warm light over the stones.
card.selfie_here: Try the Hwangnyongsa Flower Field, among the zinnia and yellow cosmos beds, with the temple ruins behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the ruins fit over your shoulder. The planting changes with the seasons, so the flowers won't always be there.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine, but please stay off the foundations, because climbing on them isn't allowed. The grounds are generally open all day, but hours may vary, so check the official site on the day.
card.challenge: Crouch down, put one big stone base in the foreground, and see if you can make the buildings in the distance look like they're at the end of a stone runway.
card.good_to_know: Hwangnyongsa was the great state temple of the Silla kingdom. Work began in 553 and it was finished in 644. The walled area covered roughly 80,000 square metres, and the pagoda stood at the centre with halls on three sides. Mongol invasions burned the pagoda in 1238, and only the foundation stones remain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk in among the pagoda foundations at Hwangnyongsa and stand right at the subject. Face along the central axis of the temple layout, with the stone bases in front of you.

card.hook: There's no pavilion at Poseokjeong, just a curved stone channel in the trees, and that's the charm. Nobles once sat along it, floated cups of wine on the water and made up poems, and you get to photograph the quiet bit that's left.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on the front (south) side of the granite waterway, the same angle as the official front-view photo. From here you look south-east towards the curved, abalone-shaped channel, with the trees of the Namsan slope around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole curve with the trees behind it. Go to 0.5x if you're standing close and the channel won't fit. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the joins between the stone blocks or leaves lying in the water.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone, then drag the slider to make it a little darker if bright leaves or sky are washing out the picture.
card.best_time: Autumn is best, when the foliage frames the waterway. Early morning is also suggested, and it's likely to be quieter. The light under the trees can change quickly, so take a few shots.
card.selfie_here: Head to the curved granite waterway, the one surviving feature of the site. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a bit low so the curve of the stone and the trees sit behind your shoulder. No guide names an exact selfie spot, so see what angle works on the day.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a designated historic site (Sajeok No. 1), so check the official site before you go for current opening times and any rules about entering the grounds.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, crouch a little, and line the curve of the channel up along a lower line so it leads the eye into the shot.
card.good_to_know: The channel is shaped like an abalone, which gives the place its name, and it's made of 63 granite blocks. It became Historic Site No. 1 in 1963, and the grounds cover 7,432 m². It's also linked to the fall of the Silla kingdom, because King Gyeongae was killed here in the 920s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, on the front (south) side of the granite waterway, the same angle as the official front-view photo. From here you look south-east towards the curved, abalone-shaped channel, with the trees of the Namsan slope around it.

card.hook: Two stone pagodas stand face to face in one courtyard, and only one of them got the fancy-dress memo. That's Dabotap, the ornate one, and it's on your right as you come in over the Cheongun and Baegun Bridge.
card.stand_here: Inside Bulguksa temple's main courtyard, stand about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Keep to the visitor areas and don't climb on or lean over any railing.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole pagoda from where you stand. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved roofs, railings and the lion. Use 0.5x only if you want the courtyard in too, and keep the pagoda away from the edges of the frame so it doesn't stretch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put a vertical line through the middle of the pagoda so the sides stay straight, and leave a little sky above the top.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can flatten the carving, so that's the time to zoom in on details instead.
card.selfie_here: Approach Dabotap from its south side, so the carvings on the base are behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the pagoda rises over your shoulder. This is our best guess for a selfie spot, so have a play with the angle.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the courtyard in front of Daeungjeon Hall, with you by Dabotap, so the pagoda is in the shot and Seokgatap and the main hall can fit in too.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine outdoors, including at the pagodas, but some indoor halls ban them, so follow the signs. Bulguksa is a working Buddhist temple, so check the official site before you go for entry and visiting rules.
card.challenge: Hunt down the one stone lion still guarding the stairs, then zoom in and give it its close-up.
card.good_to_know: Tradition says Dabotap was built in 751, in the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla. It's National Treasure no. 20 and stands 10.29 m tall. Only one of its four stone lions is still in place, and the pagoda also appears on the 10 won coin.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Inside Bulguksa temple's main courtyard, stand about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Keep to the visitor areas and don't climb on or lean over any railing.

Other pages mention the stone steps behind Seokgatap as a raised angle that puts both pagodas in one frame, and the pond pavilion Beomyeongru as a photo spot, but neither places Dabotap behind a visitor. Pages also say the pagoda is on the right after the Cheongungyo and Baegungyo bridges, opposite Seokgatap on the left. The coordinates you gave (35.79000, 129.33222) match the Wikipedia coordinates for Dabotap (35.7900, 129.3322). Sources disagree on the pagoda's height (10.29 m vs 10.4 m). Some pages recommend a tripod and early or blue-hour visits, but none states a rule about selfie sticks or tripods, so I did not list one.

card.hook: Picture two sisters standing across a courtyard: one in a showy, carved dress, the other in plain white. Seokgatap is the plain one, and it's the better model: no fuss, just clean lines against the sky.
card.stand_here: Head into the main courtyard of Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the pagoda itself. Stay near the edge of the courtyard and face Seokgatap so the whole pagoda fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole pagoda in. If you want Dabotap and the temple buildings in the same shot, drop to zoom 0.5x and keep the pagoda away from the edges, where it can stretch. Zoom 2x or 5x is good for the stepped roof edges and the lotus stones.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the pagoda up with a vertical line, and hold your phone level, because tilting up makes the sides lean.
card.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer, with softer light. Midday sun and crowds make it harder, so be patient and wait for a gap between groups.
card.selfie_here: Try the courtyard in front of Daeungjeon Hall, where Seokgatap and its sister pagoda Dabotap are both in view. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and put the pagoda over your shoulder. Standing along the side of the main hall is also worth a go, as photographers say the two pagodas line up symmetrically from there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the courtyard, halfway between the two pagodas with the main hall behind them, while you stand with Seokgatap behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the temple buildings that house the Buddha statues, but the outside areas are fine to photograph.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one centred and perfectly symmetrical of plain Seokgatap, and one with fancy Dabotap sneaking into the edge. Then pick which sister wins.
card.good_to_know: Seokgatap is 10.75 metres tall and probably dates from around 751, when Bulguksa was completed. It has three storeys on a two-tier base, with no carvings, and the storeys step in at a steady 4:3:2 ratio. During repairs in 1966, workers found relics and a woodblock-printed Buddhist text inside, believed to be the oldest surviving printed material of its kind.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into the main courtyard of Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which sits at the pagoda itself. Stay near the edge of the courtyard and face Seokgatap so the whole pagoda fits in the frame.

card.hook: Picture a small, weathered stone pagoda that looks like it's made of dark bricks, sitting calmly in open temple grounds. It has only three tiers left, but old records say it once stood nine storeys high.
card.stand_here: Walk to the front of the pagoda (분황사 모전석탑). The phone icon on the map is right at it. Face the pagoda so the flower beds are in front of you and the temple buildings sit softly behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the pagoda with the flowers in front. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Then go to 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the guardian figures, the lions and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the pagoda on one of the vertical lines and let the flower beds fill the bottom third, then crouch a little so the flowers sit in front of the stone.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer and it's usually quieter. The cosmos flowers bloom roughly September to mid-October, and the barley in the nearby fields is a spring thing.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the cosmos flower field in front of the pagoda with the pagoda behind you (best late summer to autumn). Use the front camera, switch to the wider setting if your phone has one, and keep the pagoda over your shoulder. In spring, the green barley field stretching out from the front of the temple toward the Hwangnyongsa site works the same way.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the bell pavilion in the temple grounds and face back toward the pagoda, while you stand in front of the pagoda so the whole thing fits in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active temple where photography is allowed, but please don't disturb monks or other visitors.
card.challenge: Find one of the stone lions at the corners of the platform and get it into a photo with the pagoda right behind it.
card.good_to_know: Bunhwangsa is recorded as built in 634 under Queen Seondeok, and in the Silla period it was one of the kingdom's four main temples. The pagoda is National Treasure No. 30 and is described as the oldest dated pagoda from Silla. Guardian figures flank its doorways, and a stone lion sits at each corner of the low platform.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the front of the pagoda (분황사 모전석탑). The phone icon on the map is right at it. Face the pagoda so the flower beds are in front of you and the temple buildings sit softly behind it.

card.hook: A gate is a picture frame you can walk through, and Cheonwangmun Gate is a great one. The opening pulls the eye straight through to whatever lies beyond.
card.stand_here: Stand near 해탈교, about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the whole gate fits in the frame with room to spare.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the whole gate. If you can't step back far enough, tap 0.5x, and use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the roofline level, and check the vertical edges look straight before you take the shot.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. On an overcast day the colours often look richer and there are fewer harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the pond in front of the gate (Banyayeonji Pond), where autumn leaves reflect on the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone low so the gate sits over your shoulder, then check the gate is in the frame before you smile.
card.rules_and_safety: Check access and any entry rules before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for someone to walk through the opening, keep the roofline level on the gridlines, and get the gate and a tiny walker in one shot.
card.good_to_know: Cheonwangmun Gate is a traditional gatehouse in Gyeongju. No train or tram stop is listed close by, so start from Gyeongju town and go by taxi or hired scooter. Give the name Cheonwangmun Gate to the driver or your map app.

card.hook: Picture a pond so still it looks like someone laid a second sky on the ground. That's the reward here, and you only have to wait for the ripples to stop.
card.stand_here: Stand about 85 m south of Banyayeonji Pond, right at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The pond is about 83 metres ahead of you, roughly a 1-minute walk.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view that looks like what you saw. Switch to 0.5x if you want more shoreline and sky, or 2x to fill the frame with something on the far shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the water line on one, because a tilted water line really shows in a pond photo.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is your best bet. The light is soft and calm, so you get cleaner reflections and less glare.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, turn around so the pond is over your shoulder, and hold the phone a bit higher than your face. Wait for the water to go still and the reflection will double your background.
card.rules_and_safety: Access and any visiting rules aren't confirmed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close 2x shot of the same spot, then see which reflection you like better.
card.good_to_know: A calm pond works like a mirror, so you can fit the shoreline, plants and sky into one picture. On a still day the reflection doubles the scene. Small steps sideways can move the reflection a long way, so take a few frames.
